questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Velocity Vector of a Particle Moving in Two Dimensions at a Given Time
questions.problem:
The position vector $r$ of a particle $P$ (relative to a fixed origin $O$) at time $t$ is given by

$$
r=⟨8{t}^{2},\,45⟩,\,t>0.
$$

Calculate the velocity vector $v$ at time $t=3.$
questions.worked_solution:
The particle's velocity vector is given by the derivative of its position vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(8{t}^{2}),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(45)⟩ \\  & =⟨16t,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

To find the velocity when $t=3,$ we substitute into the above:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(3) & =⟨16(3),\,0⟩ \\  & =⟨48,\,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Speed of a Particle at a Given Time
questions.problem:
The position vector $r$ of a particle $P$ (relative to a fixed origin $O$) at time $t$ is given by

$$
r=⟨\frac{{3}^{t-1}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3},5t+1⟩,\,t>0.
$$

Calculate the speed of the particle at time $t=2.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the velocity vector $v.$ Differentiating the position vector, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{3}^{t-1}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(5t+1)⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{{3}^{t-1}\operatorname{ln}⁡3}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3},5⟩ \\  & =⟨{3}^{t-1},5⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the velocity when $t=2,$ we substitute in the above:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(2) & =⟨{3}^{2-1},5⟩=⟨3,5⟩\end{aligned}
$$

To find the speed at $t=2$ we calculate the magnitude of $v(2),$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}|v(2)| & =\sqrt{{3}^{2}+{5}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{9+25} \\  & =\sqrt{34}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the speed when $t=2$ is $\sqrt{34}.$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Times at Which a Particle Is Stationary
questions.problem:
A particle $P$ moves in the $x$-$y$ plane (relative to a fixed origin $O$) with position vector

$$
r=⟨\frac{3(t-2)^{2}}{t+1},\frac{3(t-2)^{2}}{t+5}⟩,\,t\in [0,\infty ).
$$

Calculate the times at which the particle is stationary.

The particle is stationary at $t=$  
{{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the velocity vector $v.$ Differentiating the position vector, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{3(t-2)^{2}}{t+1}),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{3(t-2)^{2}}{t+5})⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{3(t-2)(t+4)}{(t+1)^{2}},\frac{3(t-2)(t+12)}{(t+5)^{2}}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

The particle is stationary when its velocity is zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =0 \\ ⟨\frac{3(t-2)(t+4)}{(t+1)^{2}},\frac{3(t-2)(t+12)}{(t+5)^{2}}⟩ & =⟨0,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

So we need

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3(t-2)(t+4)}{(t+1)^{2}}=0\, & ⇒\,3(t-2)(t+4)=0\,⇒\,t=2,-4, \\ \frac{3(t-2)(t+12)}{(t+5)^{2}}=0\, & ⇒\,3(t-2)(t+12)=0\,⇒\,t=2,-12.\end{aligned}
$$

The solution $t=2$ is the only solution that satisfies both equations, so this is the only value of $t$ when the particle is stationary.

questions.problem:
A particle $P$ moves in the $x$-$y$ plane (relative to a fixed origin $O$) with position vector

$$
r=⟨(t-4)^{3},\,(t-4)^{2}{e}^{-2{t}^{2}+3}⟩,\,t\in [0,\infty ).
$$

Calculate the time at which the particle is stationary. Do not round the answer.

The particle is stationary at $t=$
{{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the velocity vector $v.$ Differentiating the position vector, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}((t-4)^{3}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}((t-4)^{2}{e}^{-2{t}^{2}+3})⟩ \\  & =⟨3(t-4)^{2},\,2(t-4){e}^{-2{t}^{2}+3}-4t(t-4)^{2}{e}^{-2{t}^{2}+3}⟩ \\  & =⟨3(t-4)^{2},\,(t-4)(2-4t(t-4)){e}^{-2{t}^{2}+3}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

The particle is stationary when its velocity is zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =0 \\ ⟨3(t-4)^{2},\,(t-4)(2-4t(t-4)){e}^{-2{t}^{2}+3}⟩ & =⟨0,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

So, we need

$$
\begin{aligned}3(t-4)^{2}=0\, & ⇒\,t=4, \\ (t-4)(2-4t(t-4)){e}^{-2{t}^{2}+3}=0\, & ⇒\,t=4,\text{ }2\pm \frac{3\sqrt{2}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

The solution $t=4$ is the only solution that satisfies both equations, so this is the only value of $t$ when the particle is stationary.
